planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions after all danger of frost has passed once soil has warmed; give plants ample room to colonize given their large mature size.

directions: Heliconia bihai is a robust, clump-forming rhizomatous perennial native to the West Indies and northern South America, prized for its enormous, glossy, banana-like leaves and its stiff, upright, distichous bracts that unfurl in shades of red, orange, or yellow depending on the selection. Plant divisions in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, rich, well-drained soil, siting it where its considerable mature size — often 8 to 18 feet in ideal conditions — has room to spread into dense colonies. Unlike some of the more compact heliconias, H. bihai flowers nearly continuously once established in frost-free climates, making it a mainstay of South Florida and tropical cut-flower plantings, though rhizomes are killed by hard frost and the plant is best reserved for zone 10 and warmer. Feed heavily on a monthly schedule during the growing season and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring once soil has warmed; this compact hybrid establishes and flowers faster than the giant heliconia species.

directions: Heliconia 'Golden Torch' is a compact hybrid (Heliconia psittacorum × H. spathocircinata) prized for its slender, upright, golden-orange torch-like bracts held well above narrow, glossy foliage on cane-like stems. It tolerates more direct sun than most heliconias and flowers almost continuously in warm, humid conditions, making it one of the most widely grown heliconias in the Florida, Hawaiian, and Caribbean cut-flower and landscape trade. Plant divisions in full sun to light shade in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and provide consistent moisture with monthly feeding through the growing season to sustain its near year-round bloom cycle. Being smaller and quicker to establish than the giant heliconia species, it suits mixed tropical borders and large containers, though rhizomes should be heavily mulched or lifted where winter temperatures approach freezing.
